name: Mecca
span: 5th century CE – present; by tradition far older
info: Mecca is a city in the Hejaz of western Saudi Arabia, 70 km inland from Jeddah, the birthplace of Muhammad and the holiest city of Islam, whose Kaaba is the direction of prayer for Muslims and the goal of the Hajj.

facts.founded: Islamic tradition attributes its beginnings to Abraham, Hagar and Ishmael; historians note that its early history is poorly documented, and the Quraysh took control in the 5th century
facts.where: A narrow valley in the Hejaz mountains of western Arabia, 277 m above sea level and about 70 km inland from Jeddah on the Red Sea, in present-day Saudi Arabia
facts.known: The Kaaba and the Masjid al-Haram; the Hajj and 'Umrah pilgrimages; the birthplace of Muhammad; the Quraysh and their caravan trade; the conquest of 630; the Zamzam Well; the rule of the sharifs
facts.today: It is the capital of Mecca Province in Saudi Arabia, the holiest city of Islam, which non-Muslims may not enter.

t: Islamic tradition traces the city to Abraham, Hagar and Ishmael and the building of the Kaaba, while historians point out that sources for its early history are sparse and that the first clear non-Islamic reference dates from 741.
Muhammad was born there in 570 and, according to Islamic tradition, received his first revelation in a cave on a nearby mountain in 610. The city came under Muslim control in 630.
Mecca was rarely a political capital, but pilgrims kept it important, and it passed from caliphs and sharifs to the Ottomans, the Hashemite Kingdom of Hejaz and, in 1924 and 1925, the Saudi state.
dyk: A study by Majied Robinson, based on early Islamic genealogical records, estimates that Mecca had about 550 people at the time of Muhammad, while Muslim scholars using traditional sources place the number as high as 10,000.
ev: The Quraysh take control of Mecca
Muhammad is born in Mecca; Islamic sources place the failed expedition of Abraha in the same year
Muhammad emigrates with his companions to Yathrib, later called Medina
Muhammad and about 10,000 followers enter and take the city
The Qarmatians attack and sack Mecca
The Sharif of Mecca acknowledges the supremacy of the Ottoman Caliph
The revolt of Sharif Hussain bin Ali takes Mecca, and he proclaims the Kingdom of Hejaz
The Saud family takes Mecca and overthrows the sharif

sections.origins:
In the Islamic view the beginnings of Mecca go back to Adam, Abraham, Hagar and Ishmael. According to this account Abraham left Hagar and his son Ishmael in the valley at God's command, members of the Yemeni tribe of Jurhum settled with them, and Abraham and Ishmael built or, in other Islamic accounts, rebuilt the Kaaba. Islamic scholars differ on who first built it: some hold that angels did, others that Adam did. The Quran names the city Bakkah in Surah 3, verse 96, and Umm al-Qura in 6:92, and an Islamic suggestion identifies the desert of Paran in Genesis with the Tihama plain where Ishmael is held to have settled.

Historians describe the early history as largely shrouded by a lack of clear sources. The Hejaz was remote, rocky and thinly settled, and its people were illiterate, so there are few inscriptions or accounts by Greek or Roman writers. The first clear reference in non-Islamic literature is the Chronicle of 741, though Tom Holland claims that its author places the region in Mesopotamia. Possible earlier mentions are disputed. Diodorus Siculus described a holy shrine in Arabia in the first century BCE, but the place he describes lies in the north-west, in the Nabataean kingdom. Ptolemy's Macoraba was long taken to be Mecca, and Glen Bowersock still favours that, while Patricia Crone wrote that the name has nothing to do with Mecca. The etymology of the name is obscure.
sections.growth:
The Quraysh took control of Mecca in the 5th century and became skilled merchants. In the 6th century they joined the spice trade as sea routes grew dangerous and overland routes grew safer. The area was barren, but Mecca was the wealthiest of three settlements on the south-western coast, with water from the Zamzam Well and a position on major caravan routes. Goods such as leather, livestock and metals were carried to Syria and Iraq, and goods from Africa and the Far East are said to have passed through. Mecca became the centre of a loose confederation of client tribes. Once a year the tribes declared a truce and gathered there on pilgrimage, to the shrine, to drink the Zamzam, to settle disputes and debts, and to trade at fairs.

Historians disagree about the scale of the trade. Patricia Crone and Tom Holland cast doubt on the claim that Mecca was a major trading outpost, while Glen Bowersock asserts that it was. Crone argued that its trade rested on skins, hides, leather goods, clarified butter, woollens and camels, largely for the Roman army.

After Islam spread, Mecca attracted scholars, pious Muslims who wished to live near the Kaaba, and local people who served the pilgrims. Zubayda, wife of the caliph Harun ar-Rashid, paid for the deepening of the Zamzam Well and an aqueduct, in a project likely to have cost 1.75 million gold dinars. Suleiman the Magnificent rebuilt the aqueduct between 1525 and 1571.
sections.rulers:
Before Islam the Quraysh ruled the city, and their most important deity, Hubal, was placed in the Kaaba. Muhammad was born into the Banu Hashim, a faction of the Quraysh. According to Islamic tradition, he received revelations in 610 through the archangel Jibreel, and after 13 years of persecution he emigrated to Yathrib, later Medina, in 622. In 628 the Quraysh blocked the Muslims' pilgrimage, and the Treaty of al-Hudaybiya promised a ten-year ceasefire. After the Banu Bakr, allies of the Quraysh, attacked a group of the Banu Khuza'ah, allies of the Muslims, Muhammad marched into Mecca with 10,000 men and took it in 630. The pagan imagery was destroyed, and Attab ibn Asid was made governor.

Mecca was never the capital of an Islamic state except the Zubayrid Caliphate. Ali chose Kufa, the Umayyads Damascus and the Abbasids Baghdad. The Umayyads besieged the city in 683 and 692 during the Second Fitna. In 1517 the Sharif of Mecca, Barakat bin Muhammad, acknowledged the Ottoman Caliph but kept much local autonomy. The First Saudi state held the city from 1803 to 1813, and Muhammad Ali Pasha of Egypt returned it to the Ottomans in 1813. In the First World War Hussain bin Ali, the Sharif, revolted with the British officer T. E. Lawrence, took Mecca in 1916 and declared the Kingdom of Hejaz with Mecca as capital. After the capture of Mecca in 1924 the Saud family overthrew the sharif, and another passage dates the Saudi conquest of the Hejaz to 1925.
sections.life:
The Masjid al-Haram holds the Kaaba, the direction of prayer for all Muslims, and the Zamzam Well. In Islamic tradition the Black Stone was sent down from Paradise and was once whiter than milk; scientists consider it a meteorite or something of similar origin. Pilgrims circle the Kaaba, in the rite called tawaf, and walk seven times between the hills of Safa and Marwa. The Hajj, which every adult Muslim with the means must perform at least once, is held in the twelfth month, Dhu al-Hijjah. In 2019 it drew 2,489,406 pilgrims. The 'Umrah, the lesser pilgrimage, may be made at any time. Pilgrims also visit Mina, Muzdalifah and Mount Arafat.

Pilgrims came by boat to Jeddah, overland or with the annual caravans from Syria or Iraq, and many stayed. By the 19th century people of South Asian origin made up 20 per cent of the population. Ibn Battuta stayed from about 1327 to 1330 and described the people as humble, kind and clean. Non-Muslims may not enter the city. The first recorded non-Muslim to do so was Ludovico di Varthema of Bologna in 1503, Guru Nanak is said to have visited in December 1518, and Richard Francis Burton made the pilgrimage in 1853 disguised as a Muslim. The first press arrived in 1885, and the first major school, the Madrasat al-Falah, was founded in 1911 or 1912.
sections.crises:
Islamic sources place the attack of Abraha, a Yemeni ruler, in the Year of the Elephant, about 570 to 572. According to the Quran's Surah al-Fil, birds sent by God drove off his army, and Islamic tradition says this was the year of Muhammad's birth. It has been theorised that an epidemic such as smallpox caused the failure. Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr held Mecca during the Second Fitna, and the Umayyads besieged it in 683 and 692. In 930 the Qarmatians, a Shi'a Isma'ili sect led by Abu Tahir al-Jannabi, attacked and sacked the city. The Black Death reached it in 1349, and cholera broke out among pilgrims 27 times between 1830 and 1930.

Water was scarce, and floods came as well: al-Kurdi counted 89 by 1965, the worst in the last century in 1942. In 1803 the First Saudi state destroyed some historic tombs and domes in and around the city.

On 20 November 1979 about two hundred armed men led by Juhayman al-Otaybi seized the Grand Mosque, claiming that the Saudi royal family no longer represented pure Islam. They took tens of thousands of pilgrims hostage. The siege lasted two weeks and ended when a multinational force retook the mosque, with several hundred deaths and damage to the shrine. On 2 July 1990 the ventilation failed in a crowded pedestrian tunnel and 1,426 people suffocated or were trampled. On 24 September 2015, 700 pilgrims were killed in a stampede at Mina.
sections.legacy:
Mecca is the holiest city of Islam in all its branches. Its importance comes from the Hajj, one of the Five Pillars of Islam, from the 'Umrah, and from its status as the birthplace of Muhammad. The Cave of Hira on Jabal al-Nour is where Muslims believe the Quran was first revealed to him, and the Kaaba is where they pray towards. In Islamic tradition a prayer in the Masjid al-Haram is worth 100,000 prayers in any other mosque.

The built city has changed greatly under Saudi rule. It has been estimated that since 1985 about 95 per cent of Mecca's historic buildings, most over a thousand years old, have been demolished, and that fewer than 20 structures from the time of Muhammad remain. They include the houses of Khadijah and Abu Bakr, the reported birthplace of Muhammad and the Ottoman Ajyad Fortress. Two reasons are given: the Saudi government feared that such sites might become places of association in worship beside God, and many demolitions were officially for expanding the Masjid al-Haram and building hotels, apartments, car parks and other facilities for pilgrims. The city now covers over 1,200 square kilometres and its metropolitan area holds about 2.4 million people.

summary: Mecca is the holiest city of Islam, tied by tradition to Abraham and Ishmael and the birthplace of Muhammad. Ruled by the Quraysh, it came under Muslim control in 630 and later under sharifs, Ottomans and the Saudi state, and the pilgrimage still defines it.
references: F. E. Peters, Mecca: a Literary History of the Muslim Holy Land (Princeton University Press, 1994)
notes: Start 400 (circa) is a convention: the article says only that in the 5th century the Quraysh took control and the Kaaba served pagan tribes. No article gives a founding date; the Islamic tradition (Adam, Abraham) is undated. The caller may prefer another start year or a null.

Conquest of 630: the article says 'two years later' after the 628 treaty, and does not give the year 630 directly; I used 630 as the caller specified, and 'the Banu Bakr violated the truce' as the article does.

Saudi conquest dates disagree inside the article: 'Capture of Mecca (1924)' in the history section and 'Saudi conquest of Hejaz ... in 1925' in the lede. Both given in the text; the event row uses 1924.
Muhammad's birth in 570 is stated plainly in the article; the Year of the Elephant is dated approximately 570 to 572, and the link to his birth is attributed to Islamic tradition.

The article says Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr and the Zubayrids held Mecca, and gives 683 and 692 for Umayyad sieges, but says nothing about the outcomes. It says the Qarmatian sack was in 930 without details or figures, and I added none.
The Black Stone: the article says 'considered by scientists to be a meteorite or of similar origin'; given with that hedge.
The article's account of the Elephant (the 'dark cloud of small birds') is attributed to the Quran and told as Islamic tradition. The smallpox theory is the article's.

Left out: the Saadanius fossil; the present-day mayor and governor; economy, airport, railway, hospitals, sports, climate, Abraj al-Bait towers, the 2027 eclipse; the Ottoman-era Burmese community figure. The article says the discovery of oil brought immigrants, also left out.

The destruction of historic sites is given as the article gives it, with both stated reasons attributed and no verdict on the government. The 95 per cent and fewer-than-20 figures are 'estimated' and 'reported' in the article and are hedged here.
Ibn Battuta's dates: the article says he arrived 'around the year 1327' and left in 1330; given as about 1327 to 1330.

Wanted but not found: any date for the Zubayrid siege outcomes, the Qarmatians' removal of the Black Stone (not in the article), the number of dead in 1979 beyond 'several hundred', any figure for Mecca's population before the 20th century.
